newsitem.title: UK: Davies takes control at financial super regulator.
newsitem.headline: Davies takes control at financial super regulator.

text.p: Howard Davies took up the reins at the Securities and Investments Board (SIB) on Friday facing the daunting task of pushing through a huge shake-up in Britain's regulation of its financial services industry.

NewRO (New Regulatory Organisation), as it has been dubbed by officials, will bring together under one roof nine regulators including the Bank of England's regulatory department, the SIB and the existing self regulatory organisations (SROs).
Once it is up and running a single body will supervise banks, stockbrokers, financial advisers, fund managers, insurers and building societies.
It will answer one of the most common criticisms of the existing system - that its fragmented nature is confusing.
The new body will adopt the principle of lead supervision - one regulator responsible for coordinating all the regulatory relations with a company.
The structure will largely be in place by next spring, when banking supervision moves to NewRO from the Bank of England where Davies was previously Deputy Governor.
His career has also included a three year stint as Direct General of the Confederation of British Industry and before that five year as head of the Audit Commission.

The transfer of SRO staff - the Personal Investment Authority, fund management regulator IMRO and stockbroking watchdog SFA - will also take place next year although the proposed financial services reform bill is not expected to become law until late 1999 or early 2000.
By then NewRO will have taken on the staff of the Building Societies Commission, Friendly Societies Commission, Registry and the Insurance Directorate of the DTI.
The speed of the transfer is a response to concerns about the effectiveness of regulation in a prolonged period of transition.

A report by outgoing SIB chairman Sir Andrew Large to chancellor of the exchequer Gordon Brown published yesterday set out the main aims of the new organisation - to protect consumers of financial services, promote clean and orderly markets and maintain confidence in the financial system.
Another major aim will be to enhance the ability of regulators to act quickly, doing away with the intermediate tier of the SROs under the previous regime.
Until now, the SIB has only been able to become involved in many cases after SRO investigations.
Doing away with the two-tier system should allow NewRO to exercise existing powers more effectively according to Davies.
That, he argues, is more important than the notion of tougher powers.
The one exception is insider trading.
Davies has made it quite clear he believes there is a case for making that a civil offence, enabling it to be more easily prosecuted.
NewRO will have around 2,000 staff and a budget of around 200 million pounds ($327.5 million), broadly in line with current numbers across the different regulatory bodies.
It has yet to find premises but Davies' desire to be close to its 'customers' make the City - London's main financial centre - or Docklands on its outskirts frontrunners.
One question yet to be answered is NewRO's relationship with the Bank of England.

Some question the transfer of powers from the Bank of England because of the difficulty of coordinating the lender of last resort function, which remains with the Bank, and the supervision function which now goes to NewRO.
An agreement between the two, explaining how banking failures will be handled is to be published in due course.
Thursday's report on NewRO coincided with news that the government is also to introduce a tougher competition regime.
The existing Monopolies and Mergers commission is to be replaced by a new authority with wider powers.
A consultation paper will be published in the next two weeks together with a draft bill. ($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
